papers.version_note: The text is arXiv 2403.02968v4 of 14 Jan 2026 (accepted in Quantum 2026-01-13); the file name carries 2024, the year of the first version. The 'Note added' on p.11 says this version tightened the upper-bound analysis (no n-dependence in total evolution time and number of experiments) and added a tolerant tester, so page anchors here are v4 pages.
papers.what_it_is: A theory paper that defines Hamiltonian property (locality) testing, proves exponential query and evolution-time lower bounds for testing in the operator norm, gives a polynomial-cost stabilizer-state tester in the normalized Frobenius norm, and proves an exponential lower bound for learning a general Hamiltonian in that same norm.

existing.note: The abstract and Theorem 5.1 (p.37-38) state it. Theorem 5.1 adds conditions: n at least 11, trace zero, operator norm at most 1; the coherent bound is a query bound and the incoherent bound is for non-adaptive ancilla-free algorithms.
Confirmed. The formal results are Theorem 3.1 (incoherent, adaptive, ancilla-free) and Theorem 3.6 (coherent, ancilla-assisted), with conditions on k, n and the promise; see the new assertions.
Confirmed; footnote 1 on p.2 also says why: reversing time can be hard in physically motivated scenarios.

assertions.value: The authors define an n-qubit Hamiltonian as k-local if its Pauli coefficient is zero for every Pauli string of weight greater than k, and they assume without loss of generality that the coefficient of the identity string is zero to avoid global phases.
quotes: We call the Hamiltonian H k-local if αP = 0 holds for all P ∈ Pn with |P | > k.
We w.l.o.g. assume that αI⊗n = 0 to avoid physically irrelevant global phases.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper's own definition of k-locality, Section 1.1.

assertions.value: The authors define Hamiltonian k-locality testing as the task, given access to the time evolution along an unknown Hamiltonian H, of deciding with success probability at least 2/3 whether H is k-local or epsilon-far from being k-local; any output is valid if H is neither.
quotes: Given access to the time evolution according to an unknown Hamiltonian H, decide, with success probability ≥ 2/3, whether
H is ε-far from being k-local, that is,
If H satisfies neither (i) nor (ii), then any output of the tester is considered valid.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper's own problem definition, Definition 1.1.

assertions.value: The authors state that they measure the distance between Hamiltonians with the Schatten infinity-norm (the operator norm), motivated as a worst-case distance, and with the normalized Schatten two-norm (the normalized Frobenius norm), motivated as an average-case distance.
quotes: Motivated by operational interpretations as worst-case and average-case notions of distance, respectively, we focus on the Schatten ∞-norm ∥·∥∞ (aka operator norm) and
(aka normalized Frobenius norm).
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper's choice of distance measures, Section 1.1; Appendix A (p.56-58) gives the short-time justification.

assertions.value: The authors consider incoherent quantum algorithms, which perform measurements only on single copies of time-evolved states and do not interleave Hamiltonian time evolution with control operations (adaptive choices of input states and measurements are allowed), and coherent quantum algorithms, which describe the most general quantum experiments possible with access to the unknown time evolution.
quotes: On the one hand, we consider incoherent quantum algorithms, which can only perform measurements on single copies of time-evolved states, and which cannot interleave Hamiltonian time evolution with control operations.
Here, we do, however, allow for adaptively chosen input states and measurements in the different experiments performed for testing.

On the other hand, we also consider more general coherent quantum algorithms, describing the most general quantum experiments that can be performed when given access to an unknown Hamiltonian time evolution.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper's own statement of the access models, Section 1.1.

assertions.value: The authors state that their negative results cover both the incoherent and the coherent case, and that their positive results are phrased in the framework of simple incoherent quantum testing algorithms.
quotes: Our negative results cover both the incoherent and the coherent case.
Our positive results are phrased in the framework of simple incoherent quantum testing algorithms.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states its own scope in Section 1.1.

assertions.value: The authors state that the naive strategy of testing by learning with the Hamiltonian learning protocols of two cited works, applied with any norm except the infinity-norm on the Pauli coefficient vector, uses a number of queries and a total evolution time that both scale exponentially in n.

assertions.certainty_reason: A statement about cited learning protocols, argued in prose in Section 4.1 through Holder's inequality, not a numbered theorem.

assertions.value: The authors state that, because learning is a more demanding task than testing, the cited learning results of Car24 and CW25 immediately imply even tolerant Hamiltonian locality testers with the same query complexities and total evolution times, but that this works only for the Pauli infinity-norm.

immediately imply (even tolerant) Hamiltonian locality testers with the same query
important caveat: This works only for the norm ∥·∥Pauli,∞.

assertions.value: The authors state that the learning methods of Car24 and CW25 require potentially challenging-to-implement quantum capabilities such as maximally entangled input states, access to both forward and backward time evolution, and entangled multi-copy measurements for shadows, and that neither approach achieves computational efficiency even for the Pauli infinity-norm.
quotes: potentially challenging-to-implement quantum capabilities (such as maximally entangled input states, access to both forward and backward time evolution,

assertions.value: The authors state that a later cited work, ADE25 Result 1.6, gave the first efficient algorithm for learning k-local Hamiltonians in normalized Schatten two-norm when auxiliary systems are available, so testing via proper learning now applies to k-locality testing, but it needs auxiliary systems and Hamiltonian simulation and inherits an exponential dependence on k squared.

assertions.value: The authors state that the incoherent lower bound proof reduces locality testing to distinguishing the identity channel from a random rank-one phase unitary, applies Le Cam's two-point method, moves from total variation to Kullback Leibler divergence with Pinsker's inequality, splits paths by overlap between input state and measurement element, and controls the second-order term with Weingarten calculus, giving a total variation upper bound summed over queries of the form O(log(N)/d) times the expectation of the minimum of one and ε times the evolution time tk.
quotes: Next, we use Pinsker’s inequality to upper bound (the square of) this TV distance by the Kullback Leibler (KL) divergence
we can Taylor expand the logarithm to second order and control the resulting term using Weingarten calculus.

assertions.value: The authors state that for coherent testers they obtain lower bounds that are quadratically weaker than the incoherent ones, using the same distinguishing problem, and that lower bounds with the same scaling based on a simpler distinguishing problem have appeared in the quantum phase estimation literature.

assertions.value: The authors state that the hard distinguishing problem compares the trivial time evolution with what can be seen as a noisy version of it, that this noise model is somewhat artificial, and that finding physically relevant Hamiltonians for which such hardness statements can be proved is left to future work.

assertions.value: The authors state (informal efficient-testing theorem) that, promised trace zero and operator norm at most one, an ancilla-free, incoherent, non-adaptive quantum algorithm solves Hamiltonian k-locality testing in the normalized Frobenius norm using O(ε−4) queries, a total evolution time of O(ε−3), and a classical post-processing time of O(nk+3 / ε4), using only stabilizer states as inputs and stabilizer basis measurements at the output.
quotes: using O ε−4 many queries to the unknown Hamiltonian, a total evolution time of O ε−3 , and a classical post-processing time of O nk+3 ε4 .
Moreover, the testing algorithm uses only stabilizer states as inputs and stabilizer basis measurements at the output.
assertions.certainty_reason: Informal statement; the formal version with conditions is Corollary 4.3, entered separately.
assertions.reader_inference: The informal bound prints nk+3 for the classical time and Corollary 4.3 prints (3n)k+3; the two differ by a constant factor in the base.

assertions.value: The authors describe the tester: choose a mutually unbiased basis and a state in it uniformly at random, prepare that stabilizer state, evolve it under the unknown Hamiltonian for a short time of order ε, measure in the same basis, repeat a number of times polynomial in the inverse of ε, and declare the Hamiltonian ε-far from local if at least one round detects a non-locality, otherwise declare it k-local.
quotes: We let it evolve under the unknown Hamiltonian for time t = O(ε).
At the end of this evolution, we perform a measurement in the basis Bi.
then we conclude that the Hamiltonian is ε-far from being local. Otherwise, we claim that H is k-local.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper's own description of its algorithm; Algorithm 1 on p.33 gives t = ε/6 as printed.

assertions.value: The authors define two unit vectors as equivalent under a property S, a set of Pauli strings, if they are equal or one can be obtained from the other by applying a Pauli operator in S; a pair that is not equivalent is called a detected violation of the property.
quotes: We say that |ϕ⟩ and |ψ⟩ are equivalent under the property S if they are equal or |ψ⟩ can be obtained from |ϕ⟩ by applying a Pauli operator in S.
If |ϕ⟩ ≁S |ψ⟩, we say that a violation of the property S is detected by the pair of unit vectors (|ϕ⟩ , |ψ⟩).

assertions.value: The authors state that their testing protocol can be used to check whether a given unknown Hamiltonian satisfies the structural assumptions that learning algorithms need, so as a preprocessing step for learning, and, by iterating over locality parameters, to estimate the locality parameter and the resources needed for learning.
